questions.q: Which claim does Project 2's write-up make, and which does it deliberately avoid?
options: It claims the reward model is unusable; it avoids reporting the 83% accuracy
It states both the 83% held-out accuracy and the 48% adversarial-subset accuracy; it avoids claiming the model 'reliably identifies good data cleanup'
It claims the model perfectly identifies good cleanups; it avoids mentioning any adversarial testing
It claims Project 2 and Project 3 use the identical reward model
questions.explain: The claim reports both numbers honestly, since the adversarial result contradicts a claim of reliable, unbiased preference detection.

questions.q: What does the Method section trace, lesson by lesson?
options: Only the final evaluation numbers, with no earlier steps
Framing as a preference problem, building the preference dataset, training the DistilBERT-based reward model, and evaluating it on held-out and adversarial pairs
The SQL query used in Project 1
The RLHF training loop used in Project 3
questions.explain: The method section mirrors Lessons 10 through 13's pipeline: framing, dataset construction, reward model training, and evaluation.

questions.q: Why does the write-up report both the 83% and 48% accuracy numbers in the Result section?
options: Because reporting only the flattering number would make the result section marketing rather than an honest result
Because the 48% number is actually a calculation error that needs correcting
Because stable-baselines3 requires both numbers in every write-up
Because the 83% number is no longer considered valid
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states that a result section reporting only the flattering number is not a complete, trustworthy result.

questions.q: How does the write-up explain the surface-polish-bias limitation?
options: As a labeling error in the training data that should be fixed before reuse
As a genuine generalization failure: the model partly learned to associate tidiness with quality rather than the information-preservation signal the rubric ranks first
As evidence that DistilBERT cannot be fine-tuned on small datasets
As a problem specific to Cleaner A, not Cleaner B
questions.explain: The write-up is explicit that the training pairs were labeled correctly — the bias is a generalization failure, not a labeling defect.

questions.q: How does this write-up compare Project 2's reward signal to Project 1's and Project 3's?
options: All three projects use the same learned reward model

Project 2 is the only one of the three with a genuinely separate learned model trained on human preferences; Project 1's reward is computed from execution cost, and Project 3's is a programmatic execution-correctness check
None of the three projects use a reward signal at all
Project 1 and Project 2 both use human raters; Project 3 does not
questions.explain: The write-up names this distinction plainly: Project 2 is the lab's one project with a human rater in the loop and a genuinely separate trained reward model.
